From fuel prices to defensible decisions

A testable case for aviation fuel planning and Asian supply resilience.

Current maturityResearch prototypeDemonstrated calculations. Commercial value not yet validated.

The decision

When does cheaper fuel justify carrying more of it?

Fuel Atlas connects a fixed flight rotation, comparable fuel offers and aircraft constraints to explain where to buy fuel and how much to carry. The research asks a second question: when a local supply interruption occurs, does that flexibility protect connectivity or shift scarcity and emissions elsewhere?

Next milestone: an airline-supervised shadow pilot using dated contracts and approved performance data. The present system supports a diligence conversation; it does not establish dispatch readiness, customer traction or investment returns.

01

What the evidence supports

Implemented capability and the next validation step

Fixed-rotation optimization2–5 legs; explicit fuel, weight and supply constraints; matched terminal fuel. Requires aircraft-specific calibration and operational validation.
Global geographic sample67 sourced airports across six continents. Coordinates do not establish prices, supplier availability or global market coverage.
Traceable data and researchPublic benchmarks, quotation import and reproducible conditional analysis. No verified airline contract dataset, realized savings or prospective operational trial is included.

The flight optimizer, marginal tankering study and separate supply-chain planner answer different questions; they are not one calibrated global energy model.

02

A focused commercial hypothesis

Buyer and workflow

Hypothesis: airline fuel procurement teams, with flight-operations approval, may pay for faster, auditable comparisons of uplift choices. Start with one fleet type and a small airport network: reconcile offers, replay a rotation, explain binding constraints, then export the decision record.

A paid pilot followed by a subscription is a pricing hypothesis. Interview buyers and measure procurement, integration and support costs before estimating a market or setting a price.

Positioning against existing tools

Skymetrix describes fuel procurement, flight-event integration and tankering support. OpenAirlines offers operational fuel analytics and reporting. These vendor descriptions establish an existing competitive category, not comparative performance.

Fuel Atlas must test whether transparent resilience scenarios and decision provenance solve an unmet workflow. A map and optimizer alone are not a defensible advantage; data rights, validated performance and integration would have to be earned.

Economic test

Measure net value, not a headline saving

Net value = matched baseline purchase cost − feasible alternative purchase cost − additional non-fuel costs

Purchase-cost comparisons already include modeled carriage fuel; do not subtract that burn twice. Separately reconcile carbon charges, handling, displaced payload, contract penalties and implementation costs. Hold mission, payload, reserves, quote availability, initial fuel and terminal fuel constant. Report gross and net differences, rejected cases and analyst time saved. No annual saving or market-size estimate is asserted here.

03

A 90-day validation proposal

Illustrative schedule from an agreed pilot start; milestones depend on data access. These are proposed acceptance gates, not completed results.

Days 1–30

Establish comparability

Obtain authorized offers, invoices, uplift records and approved performance data. Record units, fees, validity, supply rights and exclusions.

Gate: every admitted record has complete provenance; missing inputs block recommendations. Agree tolerances and a holdout period before analysis.

Days 31–60

Replay without hindsight

Use only information available at each historical decision. Compare against recorded practice and the same-constraint baseline; independently check fuel and weight balances.

Gate: no unresolved hard-constraint violations; report coverage, burn error, reconciliation error and net value against pre-agreed tolerances.

Days 61–90

Test prospective usefulness

Run in shadow mode. Operations retains authority; log disagreements, overrides, analyst effort and data failures.

Gate: evidence of repeatable user value, affordable integration and explicit operational sign-off. Stop or redesign if benefit disappears after costs or data remain inaccessible.

04

A systems-research agenda

Compare local delivery failure, refinery disruption and a correlated import shock. Test tankering alongside ground stocks, alternate suppliers and coordinated allocation. Stocks, restoration times and service priorities must come from documented evidence or labeled scenario ranges.

Report unmet fuel and service separately, additional burn and direct CO₂, cost, recovery time and who receives scarce supply. Vary performance, logistics and policy jointly; publish model-form disagreement and scenario regret instead of invented outage probabilities. Any service valuation or equity weighting must be explicit and tested.

This agenda relates to IIASA’s work on energy, services and inequalities and systems methods, resilience and open science. It is a proposed research direction, with no IIASA affiliation or endorsement. Release code, input classifications and reproducible results; protect contract confidentiality with permissioned access and publishable aggregates.

The next decision:Secure a data partner and an independent methods review before expanding product scope. Treat empirical validation—not more screens—as the route from prototype to credible planning tool.
